primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, the symbolic 'beast' or wild animal represents earthly political power in opposition to God — specifically kingdoms, empires, and their rulers that persecute God's people. Daniel's four beasts are explicitly interpreted within the text as four kings/kingdoms (traditionally Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome), and the beast(s) of Revelation are read as a climactic God-opposing world power and/or its ruler, frequently identified with the figure of the Antichrist. The core consensus idea is that 'beast' signifies brutal, arrogant, idolatrous human government or a tyrannical ruler animated by satanic power, in contrast to the humane, God-given rule symbolized by the 'one like a son of man.'
primary_basis: Daniel 7:1-8 (four great beasts rise from the sea)
Daniel 7:17 ('these great beasts, which are four, are four kings')
Daniel 7:23 ('the fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom upon earth')
Daniel 8:20-22 (animal imagery interpreted as Media-Persia and Greece)
Revelation 13:1-10 (the beast from the sea receiving the dragon's power and authority)
Revelation 13:11-18 (the second beast / beast from the earth; the mark and number 666)
Revelation 17:3, 7-12 (the scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns interpreted as kings/kingdoms)
Revelation 11:7; 19:19-20; 20:10 (the beast as eschatological adversary defeated by Christ)

alternatives.meaning: An individual end-time person, the Antichrist: a future world ruler who embodies the beast, demands worship, and persecutes believers before Christ's return (futurist/dispensationalist reading, often linked with 2 Thessalonians 2 and 1 John 2:18).

The Roman Empire and/or a specific emperor, especially Nero: the preterist and dominant critical-scholarly reading, in which the beast of Revelation symbolizes first-century imperial Rome, the imperial cult, and Nero (666 as gematria for Neron Caesar).

The papacy or apostate church-state power: the classic historicist reading of the Reformers and continued today most prominently in Seventh-day Adventist teaching, identifying the beast with the Roman Catholic papal system across history.
A timeless symbol of all God-opposing power, evil systems, or satanic influence in every age rather than one specific kingdom or person (idealist/symbolic reading).
basis: Revelation 17:8 ('was, and is not, and is to come')

alternatives.meaning: 'Beast' as a figure for brutish, irrational, carnal human nature or humanity apart from God — used in some devotional, allegorical, and patristic-influenced readings, and in interpretations of Nebuchadnezzar's beast-like humbling.
basis: Psalm 73:22 ('I was as a beast before thee')

alternatives.meaning: Wild animals as literal agents of divine judgment or symbols of chaos/danger in prophetic oracles (e.g., 'sword, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts'), a non-symbolic or semi-symbolic usage distinct from the apocalyptic beast.

notes: There is a strong, recognizable consensus at the general level: symbolic 'beasts' in Daniel and Revelation stand for God-opposing kingdoms/empires and their rulers, a meaning stated within Scripture itself (Dan 7:17, 23). Disagreement is concentrated at the level of identification — which empire, era, institution, or individual the final beast denotes — where futurist (individual Antichrist), preterist (Rome/Nero), historicist (papacy), and idealist (timeless evil power) schools diverge. The general 'oppressive kingdom/ruler empowered by Satan' meaning is the shared core across these schools. Note that 'beast/wild animal' also occurs non-symbolically throughout Scripture; the symbolic consensus applies chiefly to the apocalyptic literature.
